name: c03-a-self-appointed-apostle.json
content:
Was Paul an apostle? He called himself one, and the church accepted the claim. His apostleship rests on a vision that he alone reported, and he was neither one of the Twelve whom ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (ʿalayhi al-salām, peace be upon him) chose nor a disciple in his lifetime. This article follows how the claim was made.

Immediately after the event of his repentance, Saul began to claim that he had received "guidance" directly from Jesus Christ. He then sought out the disciples to declare his repentance for what he had done to them.1

[paulus_figure name="bab-kisan"]Bab Kisan, one of the old gates of Damascus, now housing the Chapel of Saint Paul, which marks the tradition that he escaped the city by night, let down the wall in a basket (Acts 9:25; 2 Corinthians 11:33).[/paulus_figure]

The New Testament states that all the followers of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam at first kept away from Saul, until Barnabas came forward to believe him and give him protection. Acts records it:

26Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Ἰερουσαλὴμ ἐπείραζεν κολλᾶσθαι τοῖς μαθηταῖς· καὶ πάντες ἐφοβοῦντο αὐτόν, μὴ πιστεύοντες ὅτι ἐστὶν μαθητής. 27Βαρναβᾶς δὲ ἐπιλαβόμενος αὐτὸν ἤγαγεν πρὸς τοὺς ἀποστόλους, καὶ διηγήσατο αὐτοῖς πῶς ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ εἶδεν τὸν κύριον καὶ ὅτι ἐλάλησεν αὐτῷ καὶ πῶς ἐν Δαμασκῷ ἐπαρρησιάσατο ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ.

26And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. 27But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.2

Through Barnabas, Saul was accepted by the other followers of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam and became known as Paul. On the strength of his repentance, Paul declared himself one of the disciples of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam.

Paul's own account of the same years does not agree with Luke's. He tells the Galatians that after Damascus he went up to none of the apostles, went instead into Arabia and back to Damascus, and reached Jerusalem only after three years, where he stayed fifteen days with Peter and saw no other apostle except James:

17οὐδὲ ἀνῆλθον εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα πρὸς τοὺς πρὸ ἐμοῦ ἀποστόλους, ἀλλὰ ἀπῆλθον εἰς Ἀραβίαν, καὶ πάλιν ὑπέστρεψα εἰς Δαμασκόν. 18Ἔπειτα μετὰ ἔτη τρία ἀνῆλθον εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα ἱστορῆσαι Κηφᾶν, καὶ ἐπέμεινα πρὸς αὐτὸν ἡμέρας δεκαπέντε· 19ἕτερον δὲ τῶν ἀποστόλων οὐκ εἶδον, εἰ μὴ Ἰάκωβον τὸν ἀδελφὸν τοῦ κυρίου.

17nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus. 18Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days. 19But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord's brother.3

Acts has Barnabas bring him "to the apostles" as a new and doubted convert; Paul, who adds "before God, I do not lie," says he met two of them, and only after three years of preaching on his own authority. The two accounts cannot both stand.

Historians who set them side by side generally prefer Paul's letter to Luke's narrative, as the earlier source and the one written by Paul himself.4 Either way, the apostleship Paul claimed was established without the apostles.

[paulus_figure name="empty-stone-throne-ruins-33175020"]Stone ruins under a cloudy sky. Paul claims an apostleship “not from men nor through man” (Galatians 1:1).[/paulus_figure]

The disagreement begins earlier, with where Paul was known at all. In Acts, Saul makes havoc of the church in Jerusalem, entering every house and dragging men and women to prison, before he sets out for Damascus.5 In his own letter, Paul says that when he first went up to Jerusalem, three years after his call, he was still "unknown in person to the churches of Judea."6

A persecutor who had raided the houses of the Jerusalem believers could hardly have been a stranger to their faces. Dale B. Martin, setting the two accounts side by side, judged that they cannot responsibly be harmonised: if Paul is telling the truth, the account in Acts cannot be historical.7

Was Paul one of the twelve?

No. The Twelve were the men ʿĪsā ibn Maryam chose in his lifetime, and when Judas was gone Acts says the eleven filled his place before Paul appears in the story. Peter set the test: the new apostle had to be one of those who had been with them from the baptism of John to the day ʿĪsā ibn Maryam was taken up.

21δεῖ οὖν τῶν συνελθόντων ἡμῖν ἀνδρῶν ἐν παντὶ χρόνῳ ᾧ εἰσῆλθεν καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ἐφʼ ἡμᾶς ὁ κύριος Ἰησοῦς, 22ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος Ἰωάννου ἕως τῆς ἡμέρας ἧς ἀνελήμφθη ἀφʼ ἡμῶν, μάρτυρα τῆς ἀναστάσεως αὐτοῦ σὺν ἡμῖν γενέσθαι ἕνα τούτων.

21So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, 22beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us—one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.8

They chose Matthias: "and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles".9 Paul could not meet Peter's test, and he never claimed a place among the Twelve. He keeps them apart from himself in his own list of witnesses: the risen Christ "appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve", and "last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me".10

Was Paul a disciple, then? Not of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam in his lifetime. When Saul first came to Jerusalem, Acts says, the disciples "were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple".11 The title Paul used was apostle, "one sent", and the one who sent him, on his own account, was the Christ of his vision. The title he took for his mission is examined in [paulus_link slug="apostle-to-the-gentiles" /].

The claim to apostleship

Paul often, and without embarrassment, claimed to belong among the apostles, as in these words:

1Παῦλος κλητὸς ἀπόστολος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ καὶ Σωσθένης ὁ ἀδελφὸς

1Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,12

5λογίζομαι γὰρ μηδὲν ὑστερηκέναι τῶν ὑπερλίαν ἀποστόλων·

5Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles.13

Paul's proclamation of himself as an apostle drew no attention from the Jewish community, and the followers of the mission of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam did not believe him at all. How could they? Paul had been the chief enemy of the followers of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam.

[paulus_figure name="closed-old-wooden-door-34422178"]A weathered wooden door, closed. Paul says Christ appeared to him last of all, “as to one untimely born” (1 Corinthians 15:8).[/paulus_figure]

Not long before, he had been the one arresting, punishing and killing their brethren for their faith. The New Testament itself records that the main supporters of the mission of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam before Paul's appearance were Barnabas and Peter.

By his own admission, Paul never studied under ʿĪsā ibn Maryam and never heard any teaching from him. Yet because he claimed to belong among the apostles, the teaching he devised was crowned "the revelation of God."

The title was self-conferred, and the authority that rests on it is, ipso facto, self-conferred too. Paul explains it himself:

11Γνωρίζω γὰρ ὑμῖν, ἀδελφοί, τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τὸ εὐαγγελισθὲν ὑπʼ ἐμοῦ ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν κατὰ ἄνθρωπον· 12οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐγὼ παρὰ ἀνθρώπου παρέλαβον αὐτό, οὔτε ἐδιδάχθην, ἀλλὰ διʼ ἀποκαλύψεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ.

11For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man's gospel. 12For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.14

Paul admits that his gospel differed from the teaching of the other apostles, such as Peter and Barnabas. He goes on:

6Θαυμάζω ὅτι οὕτως ταχέως μετατίθεσθε ἀπὸ τοῦ καλέσαντος ὑμᾶς ἐν χάριτι Χριστοῦ εἰς ἕτερον εὐαγγέλιον, 7ὃ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλο· εἰ μή τινές εἰσιν οἱ ταράσσοντες ὑμᾶς καὶ θέλοντες μεταστρέψαι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Χριστοῦ. 8ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐὰν ἡμεῖς ἢ ἄγγελος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ εὐαγγελίζηται ὑμῖν παρʼ ὃ εὐηγγελισάμεθα ὑμῖν, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω. 9ὡς προειρήκαμεν, καὶ ἄρτι πάλιν λέγω, εἴ τις ὑμᾶς εὐαγγελίζεται παρʼ ὃ παρελάβετε, ἀνάθεμα ἔστω.

6I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— 7not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ. 8But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. 9As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.15
